report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Establishing Content Validity for the "Scale for Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life" (SERiEL): A Mixed-Methods Approach to Iterative Optimization
table.research_questions:
As our study does not follow an experimental design approach, we have formulated criteria rather than hypotheses to define the conditions under which content validity is deemed achieved for each item.

Content validity is assumed if the following two criteria are met:

Criteria 1: Both stakeholder groups rate the conceptualization of each item as aligned with the respective target construct. 

Criteria 2: Examples provided during the cognitive interviews align with the item definitions formulated by the research team and the items show no problems in being understood by at least 75% of the interviewed group of users.

If one of the criteria for content validity is not met, this is taken as an indicator that further adjustments to the respective item by the research team are necessary.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.q5: There is no additional blinding in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
Our study follows a mixed-methods design by combining quantitative and qualitative data analysis.  

In Part 1, quantitative data is collected through an online survey, gathering input from two stakeholder groups: researchers in the field of ER as well as users with experience responding to the SERiEL. Stakeholders are asked for their opinion on whether the conceptualization of each item is significantly aligned with the respective target construct. They may also offer comments and suggest improvements. 

In Part 2, qualitative data is collected through cognitive interviews with the user group. In these semi-structured interviews users are asked to think-aloud (Anders Ericsson & Simon, 1993) while answering the SERiEL. In addition, interviewers utilize multiple probes (Prüfer & Rexroth, 2005) to obtain more detailed information regarding the interviewee’s understanding of the items: e.g. category selection probing (“Why did you select a xy scale value? What does a high/ low scale value represent for you?”); information retrieval probing (“Is there anything you didn’t understand about the question?”). These interviews will then be transcribed verbatim and rated by two independent, trained raters to assess whether the examples provided during the cognitive interviews align with the item definitions and if any problems in understanding and/ or answering the items occur. If misalignment or further problems in understanding are observed, the raters specify the exact nature of problem. 
 
Applying a triangulation design of mixed-methods approaches (Greene, Caracelli & Graham, 1989) all results of Part 1 and 2 will equivalently be integrated to revise and optimize the items of the SERiEL-questionnaire. Results are discussed within our research team with the aim of making adjustments to items that exhibit potential content validity issues. These adjustments will be informed by the content of the cognitive interviews as well as the comments and ideas of improvement gathered in the online survey.

table.existing_data_explanation:
Data for Part 1 and 2 of our study already exists because it has been collected as part of a larger research project (Scholten et al., 2024). 

Up to the point of this preregistration only data for Part 2 was processed in terms of transcription of the cognitive interviews by a research assistant as well as coding the first 30% of the interviews to develop a detailed codebook (see supplemental material: SERiEL_Codebook) for rating them based on the qualitative content analysis by Mayring (2000, 2014).

No preliminary analysis of variables, calculation of descriptive statistics or observations of data distribution were carried out by the time this preregistration was submitted.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Researchers were recruited via e-mail. Invitations to the online surveys on SoSci-Survey (Part 1) were sent out to associates of a research initiative at the RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau, which aimed to study ER through the lens of various psychological disciplines. At the time of the invitation, this initiative had already collaboratively conducted two large ESM studies. Additionally, other German-speaking researchers with at least one publication on emotion regulation were identified through university websites and invited. 

Users were recruited through personal contact. To ensure the SERiEL could be used in both clinical and non-clinical settings, we recruited an equal number of users with and without prior psychotherapy experience. To enhance the representativeness of the user group, we ensured that users from each age decade were included, with a minimum age of 18 years and a maximum age of 75 years. The users first gained three days of experience with answering the SERiEL in their daily routines using an app-driven ambulatory assessment tool on their private smartphone named m-Path by KU Leuven (Mestdagh et al., 2023). Users were also provided a handout in which each SERiEL item was presented with additional information (label in m-Path, definition, response format, example from everyday life). Following this, they participated in an in-depth cognitive interview, where they completed the SERiEL using a specific example of their life (Part 2). The cognitive interviews were conducted in person or via (video) call and were recorded for later analysis. It was only after users gained substantial experience in responding to the SERiEL that they rated each of the SERiEL items in the online survey (Part 1).

Stakeholders did not receive any compensation.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size are 15 participants for Part 1 of the study. For Part 2 we decided for a total sample size of 15-17 participants, with the aim to interview at least one person of each age decade in both subgroups (see Data collection procedures).
table.sample_size_rationale:
Due to the absence of standardized guidelines for determining sample sizes in item evaluation by judges our total sample size for Part 1 (including both subgroups of researchers and users) was informed by Johnston et al. (2014) who recommend a minimum sample size of N = 15 to detect a large effect size of .8 in the planned analysis (two-tailed Wilcoxon one-sample test, α = .05, power = .8). Preferably, each group should be represented by 15 stakeholders.  

Due to differing recommendations regarding sample sizes in the implementation of cognitive interviews (Boateng et al., 2018; Hennink & Kaiser, 2022) we decided in favor of a stricter a priori  sampling by following the recommendations of Hennink and Kaiser (2022) who propose a minimum sample size of 9-17 interviews to reach saturation.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection will conclude either upon reaching the desired sample size or when recruitment options have been exhausted.
table.manipulated_variables: No variables were manipulated in this study.
table.measured_variables:
In Part 1, following the recommendations of Johnston et al. (2014), both researches and users were asked whether they agreed with the conceptualization of each item (dichotomous item: yes/ no), followed by a rating of their level of certainty about their answer (on a scale 0-10, 0 being not sure, 10 being very sure).

In Part 2, cognitive interviews were conducted, recorded, transcribed and analyzed by performing a qualitative content analysis by Mayring (2000, 2014). The interviews were carried out by using pre-defined probes (for further information see Study Design) in order to gain information about the interviewees understanding of the SERiEL items. The responses to the cognitive interviews were then rated by two trained, independent raters based on a codebook. Categories for the codebook were created deductively based on previous research (Mierwald & Junius, 2022) and represent the measured variables. First, the raters decide whether the example given and the thoughts expressed by the users match the respective item definition and if users have problems in understanding or answering the item (dichotomous item: problems / no problems). If there is a problem, the raters specify the nature of the problem in order to gain a deeper understanding: Expressions/ technical terms, differing understanding, incomprehension, response format, uncertainty of the answer and explanation. In line with the qualitative content analysis, three categories were inductively adapted in order to be more specific after both raters had gone through 30% of the interviews: Incomprehension or uncertainty in regard to item formulation, incomprehension or uncertainty in responding to the item. table.statistical_tests:
In order to verify the fullfilment of criteria 1 all datasets of the online ratings (Part 1) will be analyzed per item by conducting multiple two-tailed one-sample Wilcoxon tests with adjusted p-values by applying Hochberg Procedure for multiple comparisons (Hochberg, 1988). 

To verify the fullfilment of criteria 2 cognitive interviews in Part 2 will be analyzed with a qualitative content analysis by Mayring (2000, 2014) which consists of a multi-step approach to determine if each item reflects the domain of interest to a sufficient extent, if it is understood in accordance with the item definitions provided by the researcher-team and if it shows problems in being understood. The coding process consists of the following steps after the final transcript is available (for transcription process see section Transformation):

(1) Develop deductively a codebook based on previous research (Mierwald & Junius, 2022) and tailored to our research question with distinct categories.
(2) Rate about 30% of all interviews by two independent, trained raters using the in (1) developed codebook.
(3) Extract inductively examples for each category out of the interviews rated in (2).
(4) Readjust and refine the codebook according to findings in (2) and (3) through an exchange between the two raters (e.g. adapt definition of category, add or delete categories).
(5) Rate remaining interviews by two independent, trained raters using the in (4) finalized codebook.
(6) Interpret results and apply quantitative analysis (frequency of each category for every item). 
(7) Identify items which show difficulties in understanding by more than 75% of the interviewed group of users.

For Part 2  we plan to analyze the inter-rater reliability between the two independent raters of the cognitive interviews (Cohen´s Kappa).
table.transformations:
Part 1: Following the approach of Johnston et al. (2014), we will combine dichotomous and continuous ratings into a single scale. This scale integrates the certainty rating with the valence of the dichotomous rating, indicating whether each item adequately represents the intended construct. The resulting scale ranges from -10 to +10. A value of -10 represents a high confidence in the judgment that the item does not adequately represent the construct, whereas a value of +10 represents a high confidence in the judgment that the item adequately represents the construct.

In Part 2: Cognitive Interviews the audio-recordings of semi-structured interviews will be transcribed verbatim by using the software tool MAXQDA for qualitative data analysis. The resulting text files are then reviewed and revised by a research assistant. The final transcripts are then interpreted and rated by conducting a qualitative content analysis by Mayring (2000, 2014). Thereby we transform qualitative into categorial quantitative data by applying a coding scheme (codebook) (see Statistical Models).
table.inference_criteria:
The One-Sample Wilcoxon tests in Part 1 will use adjusted p-values by applying Hochberg Procedure for multiple comparisons (Hochberg, 1988) to determine if the tests suggest that the results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. 

Although there are no clear cutoff recommendations for analyzing cognitive interviews, we followed Boeije and Willis (2013) in setting a predefined criterion: At least 75% of the interviewed user group must demonstrate no difficulties in understanding an item for it to meet criterion 2 of content validity. This 75% threshold was chosen because it represents a substantial deviation from pure chance.

We will use p<.05 as a criterion of significance for the interrater-reliability coefficient.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: In order to reflect differing opinions, we have not excluded any data points. We did not apply any awareness check.
table.missing_data_handling: The online survey was set up in such a way that stakeholders could only get to the next page once they had answered all the questions. This was to prevent stakeholders from accidentally missing an answer to a question. If an interviewee in Part 2 did not provide any data on an item of the SERiEL (e.g. by skipping the item due to given skip logic), it will be marked as missed data and not included in further analysis of the respective item.
table.exploratory_analyses: As exploratory analysis we plan to analyze the comments and suggested improvements given by researches and users in the online survey (Part 1). This information will be taken into account in further adjustments of items which missed one or both of given criteria for content validity (see Hypotheses).

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .05", "p = .21"), Sentence = c("As shown in Table 6, six item wordings did not significantly differ from the expected median of Mdn = 0 (p > .05) after applying the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), indicating that participants did not agree with sufficient certainty that the item measured the intended construct.", "= .13, motives -epistemic 1, Mdn = 6.8, p = .21; emotionally pleasant situation -description -, Mdn = 9.8, padj." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Deficits in emotion regulation (ER) are widely recognized a key transdiagnostic factor in the development and maintenance of mental health problems (Aldao Dixon-Gordon, 2014; Berking Wupperman, 2012; Sloan et al., 2017). Given the complex and process-oriented nature of emotion regulation (Koval et al., 2023; Sloan et al., 2017), which involves different situational contexts (Bonanno, 2013, 2024), different motives for regulating emotions (Tamir, 2016) and a range of strategies employed by individuals (Aldao Dixon-Gordon, 2014; Sloan et al., 2017) accurately assessing these processes can be challenging (Koval et al., 2023). text.text: Experience Sampling Methods (ESM) offer a promising approach to capturing emotion regulation (ER), but item validity is often unclear due to ad hoc development and insufficient evaluation.
Qualitative approaches can uncover validity issues, yet systematic guidelines remain limited.

We examined content validity of the Scale for Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life (SERiEL), a new ESM questionnaire, via mixed-methods triangulation of qualitative (cognitive interviews) and quantitative (online surveys) data from users (n = 16) and researchers (n = 12).
Analyses revealed content validity concerns in 15 item wordings, 5 flagged quantitatively and 10 more qualitatively, with qualitative analyses yielding richer, more nuanced insights.
Most prominent was construct conflation, including confusion between ER strategies and between strategy employment and perceived success.

Our systematic cognitive interview analysis approach and lessons learned may inform standardized best practices across studies; for ER research, clearly distinguishing distinct regulation processes seems important to avoid construct conflation.

text.text: The present study aims to investigate and optimize the content validity of the Scale for Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life (SERiEL), a scale designed for ESM use.

Drawing on multiple theoretical perspectives on ER (Bonanno & Burton, 2013; Doré et al., 2016; Gross, 1998; Gross et al., 2019; Tamir, 2016), the SERiEL is intended to capture the complexity of ER by assessing regulatory strategies, situational contexts, underlying motives and the perceived success of strategies used in the context of daily ER in relation to both negative and positive affect.

text.text: To ensure comprehensive coverage, the study employs a mixed-methods approach that triangulates quantitative expert and user ratings with qualitative insights from cognitive interviews with users to examine whether each SERiEL item meets two predefined evaluation criteria, one based on quantitative data and one based on qualitative data.
Items meeting both criteria were considered to provide sufficient content-related validity evidence, while others were refined based on the collected information.
By integrating these methods, the questionnaire is intended to more accurately identify and assess ER deficits across both clinical and non-clinical populations.

text.text: The scale starts with a rating of momentary mood (rated on a smiley-based slider scale).
Participants are then instructed to recall one emotionally unpleasant situation which they briefly describe in an open-ended format.
They subsequently complete the questionnaire with reference to this situation.
The same procedure is then repeated for an emotionally pleasant situation from their day.

For each situation, participants rate their appraisal of the specific situational context, including its perceived valence, level of threat, and controllability, and, in social interactions, the intimacy and controllability of the encounter (rated on a 11-point slider scale, e.g., from uncontrollable (-5) to controllable (5)) (Doré et al., 2016).

text.text: They then indicate which ER strategies they had used (multiple-choice selection with open-ended 'others'-option).
For each selected strategy, they subsequently rate the extent to which they had used it (rated on a 11point slider scale from barely (0) to very much (10)).

text.text: Goals and Overview.
Psychological constructs assessed by questionnaires are typically defined based on the scientific literature.

However, these definitions do not always align with participants' own interpretation of given items and their understanding of the constructs, which can lead to substantial challenges in both the application of questionnaires and the interpretation of their results (Brod et al., 2009; Eisele et al., 2025).

To minimize potential bias, none of the researchers involved in data analysis had personal contact with users.

Procedure of cognitive interviews.
Users familiarized themselves with the SERiEL by completing three days of daily assessments using the app m-Path (Mestdagh et al., 2023) on their personal smartphone.

text.text: To support understanding and consistency, they were also given a reference sheet (for reference, see Supplemental Material S1) in which each item wording was presented with additional information, including a label, a definition, the response format, and an everyday-life example.
Following this, users completed in-depth cognitive interviews using the think-aloud technique (Beatty & Willis, 2007; Ericsson & Simon, 1993).

text.text: Interviews were conducted by two trained research assistants, either in person or via Zoom according to users' preference and lasted between 44 and 152 minutes (M = 77.69, SD = 33.54).
Only the participant and the interviewer were present during the interviews.
To familiarize users with the think-aloud procedure, they were first asked to verbalize their thoughts while walking through their home to count all windows.
Participants were guided or encouraged to elaborate as needed.
Users were then asked to apply the same technique while answering the SERiEL on their smartphones, using situations in their everyday life.

To further explore participants' understanding of the item wordings, the think-aloud technique was supplemented with pre-defined follow-up probes (Beatty & Willis, 2007), which have been shown to be most effective when used in combination (Boesen et al., 2018).

text.text: Follow-up probes included comprehension probes (e.g.
"How do you understand the question?
Can you give me an example?"), category selection probes (e.g.
"Why did you select this value?
What does a high/ low scale value represent for you?"), information retrieval probes (e.g.
"What did that look like in this specific situation?"), and general probes ("Is there anything you did not understand about the question?").

All interviews were audio recorded, transcribed verbatim using MAXQDA's AI-supported transcription (VERBI Software GmbH, 2025), and checked by a research assistant to resolve any discrepancies between the recordings and transcripts.
The completed transcripts were fully anonymized prior to further analysis.
As the framework of data analysis, we employed structural content analysis (Mayring, 2014 (Mayring, , 2022)), a widely applied method in qualitative research (Sigl et al., 2025).

text.text: Guided by this epistemological stance, two independent coders evaluated whether users' understanding of the item wordings and the everyday examples they provided, as captured by the interview data, aligned with the research definition in the reference sheet (for reference, see Supplemental Material S1).

The present study aimed to examine the content validity of the Scale for Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life (SERIEL), a German-language questionnaire for assessing ER using ESM.

Items were initially developed based on multiple theoretical frameworks of ER (Boemo et al., 2022; Doré et al., 2016; Gruber et al., 2012; Moskowitz et al., 2017; Tamir, 2016) and designed to meet recent ESM quality guidelines (Eisele et al., 2025).

text.text: Through a mixed-methods approach that triangulated expert and user feedback from both qualitative and quantitative data, 15 items were further optimized.

The SERIEL is now available as a comprehensive tool for clinical and non-clinical contexts, measuring ER in both emotionally pleasant and unpleasant situations, while individual items can also be used in future research.
The full scale in German (Supplemental Material S3) and an unvalidated version in English (Supplemental Material S4) will be made available upon publication.

text.text: We next explore how our analytic approach may guide content validation of other ESM instruments and interpret our findings in terms of measuring ER in daily life.

While quantitative approaches continue to dominate validity research, the present results support previous findings that cognitive interviews extend beyond the identification of general validity issues by providing more fine-grained insights into their underlying nature (Eisele et al., 2025; Schorrlepp et al., 2025; Truijens et al., 2023).

text.text: In our study, qualitative triangulation revealed content validity problems in ten additional item wordings beyond the five identified quantitatively, highlighting the value of integrating both approaches.
However, qualitative interview data require a rigorously developed analytic and reporting framework to fully realize their potential (Schorrlepp et al., 2025; Truijens et al., 2023).

text.text: Yet standardized guidelines to evaluate and optimize content validity based on cognitive interviews are currently lacking.

To address this gap, we developed and transparently reported a multi-step procedure for identifying validity issues in the SERiEL and identified key lessons to inform future validity research, particularly in the integration and analysis of qualitative data.

Within the range of available analytic approaches for qualitative research, we decided for Philipp Mayring's structured and type-building qualitative content analyses (Mayring, 2014 (Mayring, , 2022)), which represent well-established methodological frameworks for the analysis of qualitative data and have been used in validity research before (Sigl et al., 2025).

text.text: Compared to other purely constructivist approaches, the qualitative content analysis was chosen because it aligns with a post-positivist perspective, assuming that a "correct" construct definition exists as intended by the researcher (Cuthbertson et al., 2020).

text.text: This allowed for a structured evaluation of whether participants' interpretations corresponded to the intended meaning.
We found that establishing clear, conceptually meaningful definitions of the individual constructs a priori was particularly valuable in this process.
In addition, qualitative content analysis facilitated frequency-based analyses, enabling the application of cut-off criteria to identify problematic items.

However, it should be noted that the chosen threshold of 75% of participants' answers being rated as category 0 (no problems in understanding and/ or responding) was, to some extent, arbitrary and requires further empirical validation.

We initially applied a deductive approach using a predefined coding scheme to analyze the transcripts (Mierwald & Junius, 2022), which provided a useful framework for structuring the large interview dataset.

text.text: However, as the scheme was originally developed for educational contexts, it emphasized comprehensibility rather than conceptual distinctions.
Consistent with previous findings (Panayiotou et al., 2026), comprehensibility was not the primary challenge.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Panayiotou et al., 2026)</ref>, comprehensibility was not the primary challenge.

text.text: Instead, participants frequently interpreted items differently from their intended meaning, which underscores the importance of empirically assessing participants' comprehension of items rather than relying on self-reported understanding.

Although we iteratively refined the coding scheme inductively, it remained limited to distinguishing broad validity issues (e.g., differing item interpretations vs. response uncertainty) and lacked the granularity needed to guide item refinement.

This is consistent with previous research showing that cognitive interviews can identify problematic items but may provide limited guidance for improving item quality (Lenzner et al., 2023), underscoring the need for rigorous analytic approach.

text.text: We therefore complemented the structural content analysis with an inductive type-building analysis (Mayring, 2022), systematically comparing recurring patterns across items and participants to derive more specific conceptual problem types.

text.text: This two-step approach yielded a more nuanced understanding of participants' responses, revealing recurring issues in our emotion-regulation measure, such as conflating strategy employment with regulation success.
We therefore recommend extending deductive coding schemes with categories capturing conceptual validity issues.
Construct conflation, in particular, may represent a recurring challenge in ESM questionnaire development and beyond.
Future research should also examine the generalizability of additional validity categories, thereby supporting the development of standardized procedures for cognitive interview analyses.

While the benefits of incorporating qualitative data into validity research are evident, these approaches remain resource-intensive, requiring substantial time and personnel for data collection, transcription, and analysis.
Technological tools, including AI-assisted software such as MAXQDA (Rädiker & Kuckartz, 2020) may help reduce this burden.

Moreover, identifying subtle, interpretive issues require careful researcher interpretation beyond the capabilities of current AI-assisted tools (Morgan, 2023).

text.text: Although these technologies are rapidly evolving, they currently complement rather than replace direct researcher involvement in qualitative data processing and analysis.
In employing cognitive interviews, we deliberately sought to capture an idiographic perspective on respondents' item interpretations and underlying response processes.

At the same time, decisions regarding items with potential validity issues were based on aggregated patterns across participants which may be understood as a rather nomothetic approach (see e.g., Scholten et al., 2024).

text.text: Cognitive interviewing, as a qualitative method, foregrounds the premise that item validity cannot be adequately established through quantitative indicators alone, but instead requires close attention to individuals' subjective meaning-making processes (Eisele et al., 2025; Schorrlepp et al., 2025; Truijens et al., 2022).

text.text: The present findings highlight the challenges of capturing ER in its full complexity.

First, our qualitative data indicated that participants appeared to interpret continuous scales assessing the intensity of ER strategy use not only as capturing the extent to which a strategy was implemented but also as reflecting its perceived success, thereby conflating constructs that were intended to be assessed separately.
This finding underscores the importance of carefully operationalizing the intensity of ER strategies.

Given that previous studies assessed the use of ER strategies either on dichotomous items (e.g. was a strategy employed -yes/no) or continuous scales (e.g., Likert-type scales ranging from not at all to very much) to capture the extent to which individuals report using specific strategies in a given situation (e.g. Grommisch et al., 2020 , Wenzel & Rowland, 2025), this aspect should be investigated further.
text.formatted: Given that previous studies assessed the use of ER strategies either on dichotomous items (e.g. was a strategy employed -yes/no) or continuous scales (e.g., Likert-type scales ranging from not at all to very much) to capture the extent to which individuals report using specific strategies in a given situation (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Grommisch et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">, Wenzel & Rowland, 2025)</ref>, this aspect should be investigated further.

text.text: While dichotomous formats may be more economical, they often lack fine-grained detail.

This concern is empirically supported by Wenzel and Rowland (2025), who found that continuous ER items explained additional variance in affective well-being beyond binary frequency types alone, and speculated that this reflects a conflation of strategy occurrence and implementation success, consistent with our own qualitative finding.
text.formatted: This concern is empirically supported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Wenzel and Rowland (2025)</ref>, who found that continuous ER items explained additional variance in affective well-being beyond binary frequency types alone, and speculated that this reflects a conflation of strategy occurrence and implementation success, consistent with our own qualitative finding.

text.text: Therefore, when choosing the wording of items, care should be taken to disentangle these processes.

To meet this challenge, we adopted a twostep procedure: participants first indicated whether they had used a given ER strategy (dichotomous item, yes/no), followed by a continuous rating of the extent to which the chosen strategy was employed (slider scale ranging from barely to very much).
The qualitative findings further informed refinement of this item by clarifying that it assessed the intensity of strategy implementation independently of its perceived success.
The final wording was: Regardless of whether it actually affected your emotions: To what extent did you [worry]?

Second, although the literature acknowledges varying degrees of (un)consciousness in ER (e.g. Gross, 1998; Yuan et al., 2015), our interview data revealed a tendency among participants to assume that ER strategies must be applied consciously and with deliberate intention (P5: "[...] for me it's simply that influencing feelings requires you to actively do so").
text.formatted: Second, although the literature acknowledges varying degrees of (un)consciousness in ER (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gross, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Yuan et al., 2015)</ref>, our interview data revealed a tendency among participants to assume that ER strategies must be applied consciously and with deliberate intention (P5: "[...] for me it's simply that influencing feelings requires you to actively do so").

text.text: Importantly, however, consciousness in this sense should not be equated with interviewees' assumption that ER necessarily requires a deliberate intention.
ER strategies may be enacted without an active decision to regulate while nevertheless becoming accessible to awareness either during their implementation or retrospectively.

One possible explanation for this tendency to equate ER with deliberate intention may lie in individuals' emotion beliefs, which differ with respect to the perceived controllability of emotions or their perceived value or harmfulness (Peter et al., 2025).

text.text: As proposed by Ford and Gross (2019), beliefs about the controllability of emotions may shape regulatory behavior.

text.text: Viewed in light of our findings, it is also conceivable that beliefs about the controllability of emotions influence not only how individuals conceptualize ER but also the extent to which they engage in regulatory efforts.
These considerations directly informed our revision of the item wording to encompass both active and passive forms of ER (final wording: "To what extent did your behavior influence your feelings?").
For future research, it may be valuable to assess individuals' emotion beliefs alongside their perception of SERiEL items.

Doing so could help determine whether assumptions regarding the controllability of emotions systematically influence how respondents interpret self-report measures of ER and, consequently, which aspects of ER these instruments capture.
Yet, we acknowledge that self-report measures on ER remain limited to consciously accessible aspects, potentially privileging controlled over automatic regulatory processes (Braunstein et al., 2017).

text.text: Future research may therefore benefit from complementing self-report with additional data sources capable of capturing implicit processes related to ER, for instance through passive sensing via wearables or smartphones (for an overview, see Bettis et al., 2022).

text.text: Our study has several limitations.
First, because the study involved in-depth interviews with a relatively small number of participants, the generalizability of our findings is limited.
Although we sought to include equal numbers of men and women, with and without prior psychotherapeutic experience, across each age decade, our user sample was comparatively highly educated.
The researcher sample, in turn, was necessarily highly educated and embedded in academic setting due to the study design.
Furthermore, our user sample was relatively heterogeneous with regard to ethnic and cultural background, as it included only individuals of European decent whose first language was German.

Therefore, the generalizability of our results to individuals from other ethnic or cultural backgrounds, individuals whose first language is not German, and individuals with a broader range of educational backgrounds may be limited.
Second, among researchers, we did not reach the preregistered target of 15 experts.

Third, we did not follow the full procedure of the discriminant content validity approach (Johnston et al., 2014), as we assessed each item only against its intended construct rather than all constructs represented in the scale.

text.text: Fourth, the use and analysis of qualitative data are inherently susceptible to subjective interpretation, as ratings cannot be entirely free from rater bias.
Although the two raters were not involved in the original development of the scale, both were members of the same research team.
Consequently, the possibility of a favorable evaluation bias cannot be completely excluded, despite efforts to ensure objective and independent coding.

Fifth, we did not account for potential variability in how users understood and conceptualized items over time due to increased familiarity with the items or contextual factors affecting responses (Schorrlepp et al., 2025), a characteristic that may be inherent to ESM data given its repeated-assessment format.

text.text: Our current study did not address this potential for intraindividual changes in item interpretation.
Future research could examine this issue by conducting follow-up cognitive interviews with the same participants after they have engaged with the SERiEL questionnaire over a defined period.
Finally, we did not subject the refined items to the same validation procedures applied to the initial version of the SERiEL.
A systematic re-evaluation of these revised items may therefore represent a valuable avenue for future research.
The final version of the SERiEL can be regarded as a content-valid instrument for measuring ER in everyday life.
Our results indicate that qualitative data collected through cognitive interviews can effectively complement quantitative methods in validity research.
Nonetheless, a standardized best-practice analytic framework for analysing cognitive interview data is lacking.

To develop a shared deductive coding scheme for detecting item-validity problems, we propose extending other existing coding schemes focusing on comprehension issues (Mierwald & Junius, 2022) to additionally include conceptual validity issues (e.g., construct conflation).

text.text: For ER research, our findings highlight the importance of ensuring that participants distinguish between individual process components, such as strategy employment and its perceived regulation success, when answering ESM items.

Additionally, given that response patterns might be influenced by emotion beliefs, future research might benefit from assessing individual differences in emotion beliefs at study onset, prior to the assessment period.
Doing so could help render visible whether and how such beliefs systematically shape the way respondents interpret and answer ESM items.

Furthermore, our results underscore the potential of complementing everyday self-report measures with additional psychophysiological assessments to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of ER processes.
